course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Globalization
unit.description: Study how technology, disease, and environmental change reshaped the world, how the global economy and culture developed, and how people and institutions responded to globalization.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Richard Nixon, president of the United States, State of the Union address to Congress, January 22, 1970
stimulusBlocks.citation: Richard Nixon, Annual Message to the Congress on the State of the Union, January 22, 1970. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (state_union/1970-Nixon.txt, converted to UTF-8).
stimulusBlocks.note: Three months later, millions of Americans took part in the first Earth Day, and in December 1970 the federal Environmental Protection Agency began work.
stimulusBlocks.text:
The great question of the seventies is, shall we surrender to our surroundings, or shall we make our peace with nature and begin to make reparations for the damage we have done to our air, to our land, and to our water? . . .

We still think of air as free. But clean air is not free, and neither is clean water. The price tag on pollution control is high. Through our years of past carelessness we incurred a debt to nature, and now that debt is being called. . . .

We can no longer afford to consider air and water common property, free to be abused by anyone without regard to the consequences. . . . This requires comprehensive new regulations. It also requires that, to the extent possible, the price of goods should be made to include the costs of producing and disposing of them without damage to the environment.

questions.prompt: In the passage, Nixon argues that the price of goods should
choices: be set by government agencies rather than markets

include the cost of avoiding environmental damage
leave out environmental costs to keep goods cheap
questions.explanation: He wants prices to reflect the costs of clean production and disposal.
choiceExplanations: He does not call for price controls.
He discusses including costs, not lowering prices.
He wants prices to reflect the costs of clean production and disposal.
He argues the opposite.
questions.distinguisher: Nixon wants prices to include costs, not to be fixed by the government.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 9.3 key concept: the release of greenhouse gases caused global warming, and debates arose over how to respond
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing environmental debates, 1977–2015
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1977, Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement in Kenya, which organized women to plant tens of millions of trees to fight deforestation and soil erosion. She later won the Nobel Peace Prize.

By the 1990s, scientists warned that carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels was warming the planet. The Kyoto Protocol of 1997 required wealthy industrialized countries to cut emissions but not developing countries such as China and India, which argued that rich nations had caused most of the problem. The Paris Agreement of 2015 asked nearly every country to set its own targets.

choices: only Kyoto addressed environmental problems

questions.explanation: One organized local women; the other bound governments.
choiceExplanations: Both addressed the environment.
One organized local women; the other bound governments.
Maathai founded only the Green Belt Movement.
Kyoto was an agreement among governments.
questions.distinguisher: Kyoto was the agreement among governments; the Green Belt Movement was local.

He calls for action, not for giving up.
questions.distinguisher: Nixon recognized that pollution control is expensive, but he did not conclude that restoration should be abandoned.
